info.title: Effects of Self-and Other-Referencing Language on Engagement with Science Content on Social Media: A Field Experiment Authors

text.text: The present study tested whether the self-reference effect (SRE)-individuals' tendency to engage with information related to themselves-can increase engagement with science content on social media.
In a 12-week field experiment, we published 34 Instagram posts and 10 YouTube videos featuring a science lab's activities.
Captions and video titles were randomly assigned to either a self-referencing (SR) condition (using second-person pronouns), or an other-referencing (OR) condition (using thirdperson pronouns).
Engagement was assessed using platform metrics such as likes and shares.
Contrary to expectations, SR content did not yield higher engagement, whereas OR content yielded significantly higher shares.
Exploratory analyses further indicated that OR content yielded higher composite engagement scores.
These findings suggest that self-referencing language may have limited effectiveness for science communication in social media settings.
Importantly, this study opens avenues for further research on how content framing strategies influences science content engagement on social media.
Social media is a powerful tool in modern society, shaping how individuals share information and connect with others.

Its role in science communication has also grown (Brossard & Scheufelehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?L9Uxg1 2022; Mede et al., 2025) , with more researchers using platforms like Instagram, X, and YouTube to engage the public.

text.text: For scientific laboratories, particularly new ones, establishing an online presence is crucial to building visibility and outreach (Collins et al., 2016; Metag, 2020; Taddicken & Krämer, 2021).
text.formatted: For scientific laboratories, particularly new ones, establishing an online presence is crucial to building visibility and outreach <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Collins et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Metag, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Taddicken & Krämer, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, gaining audience attention on social media is challenging when competing with entertainment and algorithm-driven posts (Brossard & Scheufele, 2022).
text.formatted: However, gaining audience attention on social media is challenging when competing with entertainment and algorithm-driven posts <ref type="bibr">(Brossard & Scheufele, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, it is important for science content creators to understand what factors influence audience engagement.
One potential strategy for increasing scientific content engagement may be the selfreference effect (SRE), a well-established concept in cognitive psychology (Rogers et al., 1977).
text.formatted: One potential strategy for increasing scientific content engagement may be the selfreference effect (SRE), a well-established concept in cognitive psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Rogers et al., 1977)</ref>.

text.text: The SRE is the tendency for people to better remember and engage with information that relates to themselves.
For example, individuals demonstrate better memory and comprehension for sentences containing first-or second-person pronouns (Leonhardt & Pezzutti, 2017; Liu et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2011).
text.formatted: For example, individuals demonstrate better memory and comprehension for sentences containing first-or second-person pronouns <ref type="bibr">(Leonhardt & Pezzutti, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Liu et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Shi et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Self-referencing information also elicits positive brand attitudes (Perkins & Forehand, 2012).
text.formatted: Self-referencing information also elicits positive brand attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Perkins & Forehand, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Though the role of SRE language in social media posts has not been explored extensively, these previous findings suggest that self-referencing may be an effective strategy for increasing audience engagement.
This study uses a newly established science lab at REDACTED University in Ontario, Canada, as a field experiment to investigate how SRE influences audience engagement with its social media accounts.
We established the lab's social media on both YouTube and Instagram, manipulated pronoun use in post captions and titles, and collected audience engagement metrics.
We hypothesized that self-referencing captions and titles would lead to higher engagement metrics (e.g., likes, comments, subscriptions) compared to other-referencing captions.
The global usage of social media is continuously rising (Statista, 2025).
text.formatted: The global usage of social media is continuously rising <ref type="bibr">(Statista, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For research laboratories, social media could be a useful tool to increase online visibility (Metag, 2020).
text.formatted: For research laboratories, social media could be a useful tool to increase online visibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Metag, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Social media offers several advantages for science communication.

By allowing researchers to explain scientific concepts in accessible ways, social media can make scientific information available to audiences who do not regularly engage with academic journals or conferences (Collins et al., 2016; Taddicken & Krämer, 2021; Zhang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: By allowing researchers to explain scientific concepts in accessible ways, social media can make scientific information available to audiences who do not regularly engage with academic journals or conferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Collins et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Taddicken & Krämer, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Zhang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Social media also helps research labs increase the impact of their work.
Publications promoted on social media are associated with higher downloads and citation counts (Agarwal et al., 2016; Bik & Goldstein, 2013; Fenner, 2014).
text.formatted: Publications promoted on social media are associated with higher downloads and citation counts <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Agarwal et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bik & Goldstein, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Fenner, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, social media enhances outreach by connecting labs with potential participants, collaborators, and the broader community (Collins et al., 2016).
text.formatted: In addition, social media enhances outreach by connecting labs with potential participants, collaborators, and the broader community <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Collins et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In marketing research, social media has also shown positive effects in promoting brand image (Klassen et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In marketing research, social media has also shown positive effects in promoting brand image <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Klassen et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These features make social media a promising tool for research laboratories seeking to communicate their work, increase visibility, attract talented personnel and research participants, and engage diverse audiences.
These benefits, however, depend on whether labs can establish the necessary reach on social media.
A key barrier is that scientific content must compete with entertaining content, making it difficult to capture and sustain audience attention (Brossard & Scheufele, 2022).
text.formatted: A key barrier is that scientific content must compete with entertaining content, making it difficult to capture and sustain audience attention <ref type="bibr">(Brossard & Scheufele, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, exploring useful strategies that increase audience engagement is critical for laboratories seeking to build an effective and sustainable social media presence.
A wide range of social media platforms have been used for science communication, including blogs, Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, X (formerly Twitter), and LinkedIn.
These platforms support activities such as explaining scientific concepts, sharing research updates, engaging with public audiences, and facilitating professional networking (Collins et al., 2016).
text.formatted: These platforms support activities such as explaining scientific concepts, sharing research updates, engaging with public audiences, and facilitating professional networking <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Collins et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, each platform differs in its format, audience, and affordances, resulting in distinct strengths and limitations for communicating content (Bik & Goldstein, 2013; Lawson & Morales-Tirado, 2023).
text.formatted: However, each platform differs in its format, audience, and affordances, resulting in distinct strengths and limitations for communicating content <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bik & Goldstein, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lawson & Morales-Tirado, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, the selection of social media platforms plays a critical role in shaping how scientific information is communicated and how audiences engage with it.
In the present study, platform selection was guided by our target audience and communication goals.
As a university laboratory, our main audience was students and young adults.
The lab aimed for both rapid engagement through short-form content and in-depth communication with more elaborated content.
Based on these considerations, Instagram and YouTube were selected as our primary platforms.
Instagram is particularly effective for reaching younger audiences and promoting rapid engagement through visual and interactive features.
Demographically, Instagram's largest user group is young adults aged 18-34, well-aligned with our target audience (Statista, 2025).
text.formatted: Demographically, Instagram's largest user group is young adults aged 18-34, well-aligned with our target audience <ref type="bibr">(Statista, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Instagram supports multiple content formats, including images, short videos, and stories.
Interactive features, such as polls and direct messaging, enable users to engage with content in real time (Caspari, 2022).
text.formatted: Interactive features, such as polls and direct messaging, enable users to engage with content in real time <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Caspari, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, Instagram content typically has short visibility periods due to algorithm-driven feeds, resulting in more surface-level and short-lived audience interest (Cotter, 2019).
text.formatted: However, Instagram content typically has short visibility periods due to algorithm-driven feeds, resulting in more surface-level and short-lived audience interest <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cotter, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: YouTube complements Instagram by supporting longer and more elaborated communication.

Unlike Instagram's focus on short, attention-driven content, YouTube allows creators to explain scientific concepts in depth through longer videos,making it suitable for promoting deeper understanding and sustained engagement with complex topics (Dubovi & Tabak, 2020).
text.formatted: Unlike Instagram's focus on short, attention-driven content, YouTube allows creators to explain scientific concepts in depth through longer videos,making it suitable for promoting deeper understanding and sustained engagement with complex topics <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Dubovi & Tabak, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Youtube also includes accessibility features, such as closed captions, to help make content available to a more diverse audience.
As such, YouTube has been widely used in science communication and education (Herrington & Sweeder, 2025).
text.formatted: As such, YouTube has been widely used in science communication and education <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Herrington & Sweeder, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, YouTube has limitations.
Reaching a large audience often depends on having an established subscriber base within the platform's algorithm.
Furthermore, producing longer videos requires significant time, effort, and technical resources (Bärtl, 2018).
text.formatted: Furthermore, producing longer videos requires significant time, effort, and technical resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bärtl, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: To evaluate the impact of social media content, it is essential to quantify measures of social media success.
Common social media metrics that reflect digital consumer engagement include likes, comments, shares, subscriptions, reach, impressions, clickthrough rate, view count, and viewing duration.
These metrics can be organized into three levels of public engagement: consuming, participating, and generating (Taddicken & Krämer, 2021).
text.formatted: These metrics can be organized into three levels of public engagement: consuming, participating, and generating <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Taddicken & Krämer, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: At the level of consuming, metrics capture passive exposure and initial attention.
Reach and impressions reflect how widely and frequently content is displayed to users (Mui & Ming, 2020).
text.formatted: Reach and impressions reflect how widely and frequently content is displayed to users <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Mui & Ming, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, view count indicates whether users initiated playback.
Viewing duration reflects how long they remained engaged, providing an indicator of audiences' sustained attention (Chatzopoulou et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Viewing duration reflects how long they remained engaged, providing an indicator of audiences' sustained attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chatzopoulou et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: On YouTube, click-through rate (CTR) similarly reflects consuming behaviour, indicating the proportion of users who choose to watch a video after being exposed to its thumbnail and title (Shah & Nasnodkar, 2021).
text.formatted: On YouTube, click-through rate (CTR) similarly reflects consuming behaviour, indicating the proportion of users who choose to watch a video after being exposed to its thumbnail and title <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Shah & Nasnodkar, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: At the level of participating, metrics reflect active but relatively low-effort interactions.
Likes indicate users' immediate positive reactions and perceived appeal (Sabate et al., 2014; Kay et al., 2020), although they are often reflexive and require minimal cognitive effort.
text.formatted: Likes indicate users' immediate positive reactions and perceived appeal <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Sabate et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kay et al., 2020)</ref>, although they are often reflexive and require minimal cognitive effort.

text.text: Shares also fall within this category, as they involve redistributing existing content and are often driven by identity expression and value alignment (Labrecque et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Shares also fall within this category, as they involve redistributing existing content and are often driven by identity expression and value alignment <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Labrecque et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Subscription numbers reflect an ongoing relationship between audiences and content creators, indicating sustained interest and the potential for future engagement (Yang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Subscription numbers reflect an ongoing relationship between audiences and content creators, indicating sustained interest and the potential for future engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Yang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: At the level of generating, metrics capture user contributions that involve creating and expressing original content.
Comments require users to produce responses that reflect their thoughts and interpretations of the content, often involving greater cognitive and emotional engagement (Gavilanes et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Comments require users to produce responses that reflect their thoughts and interpretations of the content, often involving greater cognitive and emotional engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Gavilanes et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This form of engagement represents a more active contribution.
Engagement metrics also vary in their transparency.

Metrics such as likes are directly observable user actions, whereas metrics such as reach and view count depend on platform-specific definitions and algorithmic thresholds, which may not be fully disclosed.

In addition, platform algorithms influence the distribution of content; for example, a "rich-get-richer" effect has been observed on YouTube, where already popular content is more likely to be further promoted (Borghol et al., 2012).
text.formatted: In addition, platform algorithms influence the distribution of content; for example, a "rich-get-richer" effect has been observed on YouTube, where already popular content is more likely to be further promoted <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Borghol et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, engagement metrics are reflective of both audience behaviour and algorithmic amplification.
Importantly, in the present study, "success" is operationalized in terms of engagement metrics.
While these metrics capture observable engagement behaviours, they do not directly reflect how the audience cognitively processes, understands, or retains the content.
Nor do they capture important offline or longer-term outcomes from online engagement.
For example, a student may discover a research opportunity through a social media post and subsequently join a laboratory-an impact that would not be reflected in conventional engagement metrics.
Therefore, engagement metrics should be interpreted as indicators of online interaction rather than comprehensive measures of content impact.
We return to the limitation of using engagement metrics to quantify social media success in the Discussion.
To optimize the effectiveness of social media strategies in science communication, it is crucial to analyze factors influencing engagement.
Audience engagement with science communication on social media is influenced by multimodal features.
Elements like video titles, thumbnails, and leading captions act as the first point of contact and strongly affect whether users choose to view content (Foster, 2020).
text.formatted: Elements like video titles, thumbnails, and leading captions act as the first point of contact and strongly affect whether users choose to view content <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Foster, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Language and content features further shape how audiences interact with science posts.
Communicating science with clear, accessible language increases audiences' engagement, while heavy jargon use can discourage interaction (Shulman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Communicating science with clear, accessible language increases audiences' engagement, while heavy jargon use can discourage interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Shulman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Use of humor improves users' engagement intention (Yeo et al., 2020); emotional or practical content is more likely to be shared (Milkman & Berger, 2014).
text.formatted: Use of humor improves users' engagement intention <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Yeo et al., 2020)</ref>; emotional or practical content is more likely to be shared <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Milkman & Berger, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, people tend to share content that reflects positively on themselves-such as informative or "smart" content-to support positive self-presentation (Milkman & Berger, 2014).
text.formatted: Importantly, people tend to share content that reflects positively on themselves-such as informative or "smart" content-to support positive self-presentation <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Milkman & Berger, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, audiences evaluate scientific content in relation to their self-and public image.

The self-reference effect (SRE) refers to the cognitive psychology finding that individuals can better recall information encoded in relation to themselves, compared to less personal information. Rogers et al. (1977) proposed that self-referential information engages individuals' self-schemas, enabling deeper interpretation and more efficient information integration into one's memory.
text.formatted: The self-reference effect (SRE) refers to the cognitive psychology finding that individuals can better recall information encoded in relation to themselves, compared to less personal information. <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Rogers et al. (1977)</ref> proposed that self-referential information engages individuals' self-schemas, enabling deeper interpretation and more efficient information integration into one's memory.

text.text: As a result, phrases involving information that cues oneself become more distinctive and more easily recalled.
Self-reference is typically experimentally induced by manipulating pronouns.
For example, Shi et al. (2011) had participants view everyday object nouns preceded by either a first-person ("my") or third-person ("his") possessive pronoun.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Shi et al. (2011)</ref> had participants view everyday object nouns preceded by either a first-person ("my") or third-person ("his") possessive pronoun.

text.text: During a surprise recall test, nouns paired with first-person possessive pronouns were recalled more accurately than those paired with third-person pronouns.
Beyond memory, self-referential content can also shape people's attitudes toward brands.
In a study by Perkins and Forehand (2012), participants learned two artificial brand families paired with either first-person or third-person pronouns.
text.formatted: In a study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Perkins and Forehand (2012)</ref>, participants learned two artificial brand families paired with either first-person or third-person pronouns.

text.text: Self-associated brands were later categorized more quickly and evaluated more positively than otherassociated brands.
On social media, self-referential language has been used as a marketing strategy to engage audiences.

Self-relevant language use helps capture consumers' attention and increase their psychological closeness to the message source (Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010). Cruz and Pezzuti (2017) examined more than 15,000 Facebook marketing posts and found that messages containing second-person pronouns (e.g., you, your) generated significantly higher levels of engagement metrics, including likes, comments, and shares, compared to messages without pronouns (e.g., "Think of all information that is saved on your computer" versus "Think of all information that is saved on the computer").
text.formatted: Self-relevant language use helps capture consumers' attention and increase their psychological closeness to the message source <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Cruz and Pezzuti (2017)</ref> examined more than 15,000 Facebook marketing posts and found that messages containing second-person pronouns (e.g., you, your) generated significantly higher levels of engagement metrics, including likes, comments, and shares, compared to messages without pronouns (e.g., "Think of all information that is saved on your computer" versus "Think of all information that is saved on the computer").

text.text: Second-person pronouns prompted consumers to think about the message in relation to themselves, which encouraged self-relevant processing and enhanced engagement with the content.

Self-referential language can have varied effects depending on the message content and the engagement metrics being examined. Labrecque et al. (2020) analyzed Facebook posts from 90 consumer brands, and found that second-person pronouns were most strongly associated with increases in comments, but showed less consistent effects on likes and shares.
text.formatted: Self-referential language can have varied effects depending on the message content and the engagement metrics being examined. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Labrecque et al. (2020)</ref> analyzed Facebook posts from 90 consumer brands, and found that second-person pronouns were most strongly associated with increases in comments, but showed less consistent effects on likes and shares.

text.text: These effects further varied by product type.
For utilitarian products, chosen for functional or practical reasons, second-person pronouns increased likes and comments but were associated with fewer shares.
For hedonic products, linked to enjoyment or leisure, second-person pronouns reduced sharing compared to third-person pronouns.
Despite previous studies demonstrating that self-referential language can enhance memory, attitudes, and engagement, its use in science communication on social media remains unclear.

With research laboratories increasingly relying on social media to engage with public audiences, yet typically lacking the resources to promote content through paid advertising, language-based strategies such as self-referential framing represent a potentially low-cost approach to increasing visibility and engagement.
Because science communication differs from marketing in its goals and audience expectations, it is unclear whether findings from commercial contexts will generalize to scientific domains.
The present study therefore investigates whether self-referential language increases audience engagement with science content on social media.

We use a new cognitive neuroscience lab at REDACTED University as a field experiment to explore whether self-referential video titles and photo captions enhance audience engagement with science content on YouTube and Instagram.

We hypothesize that videos and posts with SRE titles and captions will score higher on engagement metrics (e.g., likes, shares, subscription, reach), compared to those with other-referencing titles and captions.
The first author created new YouTube and Instagram accounts for the lab and an introductory post that is excluded from the study.
To build an initial audience, the accounts followed relevant accounts within the lab's professional network and were promoted at an academic conference.
At the start of data collection, the Instagram account had 43 followers and the YouTube account had 2 followers.
Content creation and posting occurred over a 12-week period from November 2024 to February 2025.
Content covered four thematic categories: (1) lab research highlights, (2) behind-the-scenes events, (3) daily life in the lab, and (4) expert interviews.
Posting time and frequency were held constant on both platforms.
On Instagram, a total of 34 posts were published, comprising 24 photo posts and 10 videos (reels).
Photo posts were published weekly on Mondays and Wednesdays around 1:00 pm, while videos were posted weekly on Sundays around 3:00 pm.
On YouTube, the same 10 videos were published weekly on Sundays around 3:00 pm, matching the Instagram reels in content and posting time.
All videos were produced with comparable lengths (ranging from 6 min 13 s to 7 min 5 s) and used a consistent title font, thumbnail style, and ending logo.
For each post, two caption versions were prepared prior to publication: one using selfreferential (SR) language and one using other-referential (OR) language.
SR captions used pronouns that directly addressed the audience (e.g., you, your, we).
OR captions replaced audience-directed pronouns with third-person references (e.g., the lab, students, listeners).
Across conditions, captions were matched with content, grammatical structure, and pronoun frequency.
For example: SR: "Here's your inside look at the Synaptic Rodeo show!
Your gaze changes dynamically with music."
OR: "Here's the lab's inside look at the Synaptic Rodeo show!
The audience's gaze changes dynamically with music."
The 34 Instagram photo posts were then randomly assigned to either the SR or OR condition to determine which caption version was used for posting.
Each condition has a total of 17 posts, including 12 photo posts and 5 video posts.
The thematic category of these posts was relatively balanced across conditions and was not directly manipulated.
For Youtube videos, two title versions (SR and OR) were also created in addition to descriptions for each video, again controlling for sentence structure and only differing in pronoun use.
For example: SR: "Your 33 Questions with Dr.
REDACTED FOR PEER REVIEW" OR: "REDACTED FOR PEER REVIEW Lab's 33 Questions with Dr.
REDACTED" Each YouTube video was assigned to the same condition and has identical descriptions as its corresponding Instagram video post.
Audience engagement was measured via metrics provided by Instagram Insights and YouTube Analytics, the inbuilt tracking tools of both platforms.

text.text: To test the hypothesis that posts with SR captions receive higher audience engagement metrics than those with OR captions, we conducted 2*2 ANOVAs (SR/OR and post/video) on Instagram metrics.

A sensitivity power analysis indicated that, given the current sample size (α = .05, power = .80), the study was powered to detect effects of at least η² = .21, corresponding to a large effect size; we therefore had limited sensitivity to detect small or medium effects.
The caption condition had a large effect on the number of shares (F(1) = 6.229, p = .018, η² = .17; see Fig. 1).
text.formatted: The caption condition had a large effect on the number of shares (F(1) = 6.229, p = .018, η² = .17; see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: However, the effect went in the opposite direction of the hypothesis: OR posts were shared on average 2.29 times (SD = 2.49), while SR posts were only shared 0.59 times (SD = 1.18).
There was no significant main or interaction effect of post format (photo or video).
The other metrics (likes, reach, and SG) were not significantly affected by condition or format (all p > .28; see full ANOVA tables S1a-S1d).

A post-hoc descriptive analysis examined potential relationships between other Instagram post characteristics and audience engagement (see supplemental figures S3-S12).
"Behind-the-scenes" posts generally demonstrated higher reach, shares, and subscriber growth and general engagement score.
"Daily life in the lab" posts demonstrate moderate and relatively consistent engagement across posts.
Lab "research highlights" and "expert interviews" generally demonstrated lower overall engagement, despite a few high-performing outlier posts.
Posts containing two or more visible faces generally demonstrated below-average general engagement scores.
All five of the highest-ranking posts have only one visible face within the thumbnail.
Posts featuring eye-tracking glasses, the lab's signature technology, demonstrated higher reach and shares.
However, the two posts with the highest overall engagement score did not contain eye-tracking glasses.
Posts with visible technological equipment demonstrated lower shares and engagement rankings compared to posts without equipment.
Posts using thumbnails photographed in natural settings (see Figure 9) without digitally designed graphic elements generally demonstrated higher numbers of likes.

text.text: We investigated whether social media captions using self-referential (SR) language lead to better audience engagement with scientific content.

Although SR language has been associated with enhanced engagement in cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and marketing contexts (Cruz & Pezzuti, 2017; Leonhardt & Pezzutti, 2017; Liu et al., 2023; Perkins & Forehand, 2012; Shi et al., 2011; Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010), the present findings suggest that SR effects may not generalize to science communication on social media.
text.formatted: Although SR language has been associated with enhanced engagement in cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and marketing contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Cruz & Pezzuti, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Leonhardt & Pezzutti, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Liu et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Perkins & Forehand, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Shi et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010)</ref>, the present findings suggest that SR effects may not generalize to science communication on social media.

text.text: On Instagram, SR captions did not show a significant advantage over OR captions in any of the four engagement metrics.
Instead, we found that posts with OR captions received significantly more shares.
OR-captioned posts also ranked higher on the general engagement PCA metric.
One possible explanation is our audiences' motivation to engage with infotainment content.

For engagement driven by audience enjoyment, as opposed to practical utility, an overuse of self-referencing pronouns could backfire and lead to less optimal engagement (Labrecque et al., 2020), potentially reducing perceptions of content credibility and emotional appeal.
text.formatted: For engagement driven by audience enjoyment, as opposed to practical utility, an overuse of self-referencing pronouns could backfire and lead to less optimal engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Labrecque et al., 2020)</ref>, potentially reducing perceptions of content credibility and emotional appeal.

text.text: Another possible reason is the limited sample size of our posts due to time and resource constraints.
The study was only adequately powered to detect large effects, and may therefore have been unable to identify smaller but potentially meaningful effects.
On YouTube, videos with OR titles and captions had higher mean values on the engagement metrics watch time, impressions, views, and unique viewers.
SR captions showed higher mean click-through rates (CTR) than OR captions; however, this pattern is likely influenced by how CTR is calculated (clicks divided by impressions).
Because OR captions generated higher impressions, the denominator in the CTR calculation increased, which explains the lower CTR.
Our exploratory evidence suggests that OR captions may enhance engagement with scientific communication.
One potential advantage of OR language is its ability to foster a shared perspective between the communicator and the audience (Clark & Brennan, 1991).
text.formatted: One potential advantage of OR language is its ability to foster a shared perspective between the communicator and the audience <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clark & Brennan, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Third-person pronouns may present information as broadly relevant, allowing content to appeal to a wider audience rather than targeting viewers with direct or personal experience related to the message.
Conversely, SR language may unintentionally alienate some readers who do not directly identify with the communicator's experiences.
In this study, many posts highlighted lab events that occurred in specific physical settings.
In these contexts, SR language may have only been relatable to individuals who directly attended these events.
In addition, third-person pronouns may signal objectivity, authority, and credibilityqualities that are central to effective science communication (Fiske & Dupree, 2014).
text.formatted: In addition, third-person pronouns may signal objectivity, authority, and credibilityqualities that are central to effective science communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fiske & Dupree, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Given that the primary audience of our posts consisted of scientists, students, and science enthusiasts, their preference for OR language may reflect alignment with academic communication norms, which typically emphasize objectivity over personal narrative.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the "REDACTED FOR PEER REVIEW Lab" name as part of the OR language may have introduced a brand-related effect that could have influenced engagement outcomes.
Comparing media formats, photo posts gained an overall higher engagement than video among Instagram users.
Our results align with prior research demonstrating that photos often outperform videos in scientific education contexts on Instagram (Kauffman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Our results align with prior research demonstrating that photos often outperform videos in scientific education contexts on Instagram <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kauffman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Photos are more accessible to users who may be unable to play videos aloud, require less sustained attention, and support self-paced learning (Kauffman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Photos are more accessible to users who may be unable to play videos aloud, require less sustained attention, and support self-paced learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kauffman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, our videos (around 7 minutes) were significantly longer than typical Instagram reels (under 30 seconds), potentially making them less aligned with platformspecific audience expectations and contributing to lower performance.
Comparing platforms, Instagram generated higher engagement than YouTube.
This difference may be attributed to Instagram's large student user base (Pavelle & Wilkinson, 2020).
text.formatted: This difference may be attributed to Instagram's large student user base <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Pavelle & Wilkinson, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In our experience, it was easier to connect and collaborate with other students, scientists, and organizations on Instagram.

Moreover, Instagram's interactive functionalities, such as sharing posts through private messages, posting collaborative content with other accounts, and receiving story mentions may have further amplified engagement.

In contrast, YouTube visibility tends to be more dependent on an established subscriber base and accumulated views, making it difficult for newer or smaller channels to gain traction (Burgess & Green, 2009).
text.formatted: In contrast, YouTube visibility tends to be more dependent on an established subscriber base and accumulated views, making it difficult for newer or smaller channels to gain traction <ref type="bibr">(Burgess & Green, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Subscriber growth on Instagram, and views and unique viewers on YouTube, increased over the time of the data collection.
In contrast, most other engagement metrics remained relatively stable over time, with most of the audience interaction occurring within the first day of posting.
This pattern suggests that social media engagement for science content tends to be immediate, likely driven by algorithmic promotion of fresh content and audiences' habitual consumption of new posts.

There was no evidence that posts created later in the data collection period performed better, suggesting that a growing number of subscribers (at least in the lower three-digit range) did not substantially amplify engagement.
This study further explored how content-related characteristics were associated with audience engagement on Instagram.
These findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.
The top-performing posts highlight the importance of interactivity.
The highest-ranking post was related to a conference at which the account had been shared, and this prior interaction with the target audience may have contributed to higher engagement.
The second-highest-ranking post was a quiz-style post inviting audiences to guess a Christmas song, and thus its interactive format may have contributed to its popularity.
Overall, posts featuring behind-the-scenes content tended to demonstrate higher engagement.
One possible explanation is that BTS posts often feature event-based or experiential content, which may enhance perceived novelty.
Such content may provide audiences with a sense of "insider access" to scientific activities that are not routinely visible, thereby increasing its shareability and engagement potential.
Posts with a single visible face in the thumbnail tended to receive more engagement compared to posts with multiple or no visible faces.

Since human faces are strong visual cues that quickly attract attention on social media (Bakhshi, Shamma, & Gilbert, 2014), posts with faces may be more likely to draw viewer attention than those without faces.
text.formatted: Since human faces are strong visual cues that quickly attract attention on social media <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bakhshi, Shamma, & Gilbert, 2014)</ref>, posts with faces may be more likely to draw viewer attention than those without faces.

text.text: On the other hand, multiple faces may create competing focal points within the same image, making it harder for viewers to quickly identify a key element in a fast-scrolling social media environment.
Findings related to technological equipment were mixed.

Technological equipment may increase perceived novelty, but may also make the content less immediately accessible to broader audiences, as images of unfamiliar research tools can require more cognitive effort.
Finally, posts using natural photographic thumbnails generally demonstrated higher engagement compared to posts with digital or graphic-based designs.
This may reflect perceived authenticity and visual processing fluency, as natural imagery is often processed more effortlessly and may be perceived as more genuine.

Prior research suggests that perceived authenticity can play an important role in audience engagement and trust formation, which could translate to better engagement measures (Morhart et al., 2015; Zhang, 2026).

text.text: These findings suggest that beyond SR/OR language in post captions, factors such as format, content, and platform also play important roles in shaping engagement with science communication on social media, providing directions for future research.

To ensure the validity of the findings of this field experiment, potentially confounding variables such as posting times, caption structures, and video format were carefully controlled, allowing observed differences in engagement to be more confidently attributed to the self-referencing manipulation.
Despite these precautions, some potential limitations should be considered.
One major limitation is the influence of platform recommendation algorithms on post visibility.
Engagement metrics do not purely reflect audience interest, as they are also heavily shaped by algorithmic decisions that promote or suppress content.
Certain posts might receive disproportionate visibility for reasons unrelated to content quality or language conditions.
In addition, social media platforms do not fully disclose formulas used to generate engagement metrics, further complicating the interpretation of these metrics.
Another limitation is that the current metrics do not capture all dimensions of audience engagement.
While these metrics provide indirect indicators of audience motivation, attitude, and interest, they do not directly assess emotional responses or deeper processing of content.
In this study, the comments were excluded from analyses due to a floor effect.
Because comments often reflect deeper cognitive or emotional engagement, the low comment frequency may indicate that observed engagement primarily represents surface-level interaction.
Future studies could incorporate alternative measures, such as surveys or physiological assessments, to provide a deeper understanding of audience engagement.

It would also be valuable to collect metrics involving real-world uptake of social media content (e.g., tracking the number of new participants signing up to participate in the lab's research, or the number of new students applying to work in the lab).
Such metrics would require more involvement from the researchers but may ultimately be more meaningful in informing whether science communication via social media translates to real-world impact.
Future research should further investigate the effectiveness of OR captions in enhancing audience engagement.
Exploring the potential brand effect of including the lab's name in captions versus neutral other-referencing pronouns is another promising direction.
To address existing limitations, future field experiments should incorporate larger sample sizes while keeping a tight control on extraneous factors
For researchers, the costs of managing a lab's social media presence must be weighed against the potential benefits.
Science communication on social media requires substantial effort, from account creation and promotion to content planning, filming, editing, and caption writing.
In addition, social media management involves ongoing engagement with other organizations, promoting events , and interacting with audiences.
Given that many research laboratories lack dedicated social media personnel, these responsibilities often compete with other research priorities (Banse et al., 2026; Calice et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Given that many research laboratories lack dedicated social media personnel, these responsibilities often compete with other research priorities <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Banse et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Calice et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Labs with limited resources may therefore struggle to maintain an active presence.
Labs with extensive resources may question if social media content creation is the best use of grant funding and aligned with tax-payer priorities.
Despite these challenges, social media remains a valuable tool for science communication.
In this field experiment, the lab's social media presence supported outreach and engagement with scientific content.
Anecdotally, conversations with students suggest that social media has helped spark interest in the lab, with some students asking questions or reaching out to learn more.

The lab has also used its social media accounts to share lab-related events and connect with scientists beyond its immediate geographic area, suggesting potential benefits of social media beyond the engagement measured in this study.
With social media playing an expanding role in public engagement with science, understanding strategies influencing audience engagement is crucial.
This study found no overall engagement advantage of self-referencing language compared to otherreferencing language.
In fact, captions using OR language resulted in significantly higher sharing behaviour on Instagram and showed potential for increasing engagement on YouTube.

This study contributes to a growing understanding of how language strategies can be leveraged to enhance the reach and impact of science communication on social media platforms, and provides practical guidance for scientists seeking to maximize the visibility and accessibility of their work online.

We conducted an exploratory factor analysis to explore the aggregated effect of the metrics we collected for each platform.
We examined the same metrics as before and included only day data for each post.

To understand the interrelationship across metrics and their fit for factor analysis, we created a correlation matrix across metrics and calculated the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) values for each platform.

The KMO statistic evaluates whether the observed correlations among variables are sufficiently strong to support factor analysis, with higher values indicating greater shared variance among variables and better suitability for factor extraction.
For Instagram metrics (Figure S1), likes were strongly correlated (r=0.59) with reach and moderately correlated (r=0.44) with shares.

text.text: There was also a strong positive correlation (r=0.62) between reach and shares.
SG showed weak correlations with the other three metrics (all r < 0.3).

text.text: While all four metrics had KMO values above 0.6, indicating adequate sampling adequacy for factor analysis, we excluded SG from the factor analysis to improve the fit of the general factor model and enhance interpretability.
For YouTube metrics (Figure S2), there was a strong negative correlation between impressions and CTR (r = -0.81).

text.text: A strong positive correlation was observed between likes and views (r = 0.90), likes and unique viewers (r = 0.74), and views and unique viewers (r = 0.82).
A medium positive correlation was found between CTR and average watch time (r = 0.66).
We retained the metrics with KMO values greater than 0.5 in the factor analysis, which left likes, views, impressions, and unique viewers.
We then conducted principal component analysis and extracted a general engagement factor that accounts for most of the variance for each of the metrics included in the two platforms, respectively.
This general factor explained 67% of the variance in Instagram metrics, with reach having the highest loading (r=0.88).
For YouTube metrics, the general factor explained 74% of the variance, with views and unique viewers having the highest loading (r=0.97).
